name: Wien's Displacement Law
statement: The hotter a body, the shorter the wavelength at which it glows most brightly.
statementAccent: the shorter the wavelength at which it glows most brightly
meaning: The peak of a black body's radiation shifts toward shorter wavelengths as it heats up. A warming object glows red, then orange, yellow, white, and finally blue-white — so the colour of a glowing body is a direct thermometer of its temperature.
mechanism: The peak wavelength times the absolute temperature equals a fixed constant, Wien's displacement constant of about 2.9 millimetre-kelvin. This follows from Planck's law: differentiating the black-body spectrum and finding its maximum gives the constant, so as temperature rises the peak wavelength falls in inverse proportion.

examples.text: Cool stars look red, hotter ones white, and the hottest blue — so a star's colour reads its surface temperature, the red of Betelgeuse against the blue-white of Rigel.
At a surface temperature near 5,800 kelvin the Sun peaks in visible light, around 500 nanometres — the reason its output coincides with the band our eyes evolved to see.
Near-room-temperature objects peak deep in the infrared, around ten micrometres, invisible to the eye — the wavelength band thermal cameras are built to detect.

variants.name: Planck's law
variants.text: The full spectral distribution of which the displacement law simply locates the peak; it is the maximum of the Planck curve.

variants.name: Wien's approximation
variants.text: A separate 1896 result, sometimes also called 'Wien's law': an approximate formula for the whole spectrum that fits the short-wavelength end but fails at long wavelengths — not to be confused with the displacement law.

whyItMatters: It turns colour into a temperature gauge, foundational to astronomy — reading stellar temperatures from starlight — and to thermal imaging and pyrometry. Together with the Stefan–Boltzmann and Planck laws it completes the classical description of how hot bodies glow.

working.text: estimate a black body's temperature from where its emission peaks — bluer means hotter, redder means cooler.
choose a sensor for the wavelength band where the target actually peaks, which for near-room-temperature objects is the infrared.

working.lead: Specify the parameterisation of the peak
working.text: state whether you mean the peak per wavelength or per frequency, since the two differ and do not convert by the simple wavelength-frequency relation.

limits: The law holds strictly only for an ideal black body; real emitters with wavelength-dependent emissivity deviate. There is also a genuine subtlety: the spectrum peaks at a different place depending on whether it is plotted per unit wavelength or per unit frequency, because converting a spectral density introduces a Jacobian factor — so 'the wavelength of maximum emission' is ambiguous until the parameterisation is specified. Its constant is now exact by definition, and it is confirmed continually by spectroscopy and astronomy.
misreadings: It is not the same as Wien's approximation of 1896, a distinct formula for the whole spectrum that fails at long wavelengths. And the 'peak wavelength' is not a single unambiguous quantity — it depends on whether the spectrum is measured per wavelength or per frequency, which peak at different places.
origin: Derived by the German physicist Wilhelm Wien in 1893, building on earlier observations by Samuel Langley. Wien received the 1911 Nobel Prize for his black-body work; the displacement law was later placed on rigorous footing as a consequence of Planck's law.

sources.text: Wien, W. (1896). “Ueber die Energievertheilung im Emissionsspectrum eines schwarzen Körpers.” Annalen der Physik, vol. 294. — the paper giving the distribution law that bears his name.
Wien's displacement law, Wikipedia. — the statement, the constant, and the per-wavelength/per-frequency peak subtlety.
Wien approximation, Wikipedia. — the distinct 1896 short-wavelength formula that shares the name.
